name: Emeka Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Emeka, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach chemistry at Northgate Academy, a big secondary school with about thirteen hundred students, ages eleven to eighteen. A normal day is five lessons, usually two of them practicals, so I'm setting out test tubes and goggles at eight and scrubbing burnt copper sulphate off benches at four. I love the practicals, when a Year 9 sees a flame go green and actually says wow. What wears me out is data drops: entering grades into the system every six weeks so the trust can make charts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside school? Who's at home, and how are you fixed for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya, who's a junior solicitor at a firm in town, mostly reading contracts and doing research for the partners. We rent a one-bed near the station and we've saved about four months of bills, which we're slowly turning into a deposit. I'm a union member, not a loud one. I use the AI chatbot now and then to make three versions of a worksheet, once my colleague Hannah showed me it actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy tool and not much more. I'd probably joke in the department that we can stop going to the training sessions on it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's pretty much fine for me. Chemistry teachers are always short, the trust needs us, and the pay rises are small but steady. Priya's firm would carry on as before too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: teach, run the practicals, use the chatbot for worksheet versions. We'd keep putting three hundred a month towards the deposit. Maybe I'd go for second in department in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like a weather forecast that says cloudy all week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture, even with AI going nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust's budget. They keep merging small A-level groups to save money, and if chemistry gets merged with the school down the road, someone travels. But that's been on the cards for years, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the chatbot for worksheets. Would you keep doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it saves me maybe an hour a week. It's not life-changing. AI is like the good photocopier at school: you only notice when it's broken.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **handy tool** and not much more.
I'd joke that the department can skip the **training sessions** now.
think: I think chemistry teachers are **always short**, so my job and steady pay feel safe.
Priya's **law firm** would carry on as before, so our household is fine.
do: Keep teaching chemistry and using the chatbot for **worksheet versions**.
Put **£300 a month** towards a flat deposit with Priya.
Aim for **second in department** within a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, if a little flat, like a forecast that says cloudy all week.
S0.quote: AI is like the good photocopier at school: you only notice when it's broken.
fieldNote: His security comes from **shortage subject** status; chemistry teachers are hard to replace.
The only live worry is the trust **merging A-level groups**, which predates AI.
Uses AI lightly and **practically**, adopted once a trusted colleague proved it.

steps.text: Keep running chemistry practicals and teaching five lessons a day
Keep using the chatbot to make three worksheet versions
Save £300 a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers need a say in how this gets used, and the time saved should go back to students, not into bigger classes. I'd say that at union meetings and probably on the staff survey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the data drops and report writing get automated, which is great, but the trust will want something back for it, probably a sixth lesson. The bigger worry is Priya. Contract checking is exactly the stuff on that list, and that's what my girlfriend Priya does all day at the law firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the trust's AI training properly this time, not just sit through it, because once it's proven I'd rather be good at it. I'd push in the union for a rule that saved time stays with teachers. And we'd pause the deposit and keep the four months as a proper emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Quite good about my own job, and a knot in my stomach about Priya's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about your job. What about Priya's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her firm's already talking about hiring fewer trainees. If she drops to four days or loses her job, we'd be on my salary alone, which covers rent and bills but nothing else. She's sharp though; she'd find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if her hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, first. We'd stop looking at places. Then the gym memberships and the car, which we barely use anyway. I'd sell the car before I touched the emergency fund.

say: I'd say teachers need a **say** in how AI is used in school.
Time saved should go back to **students**, not into bigger classes.
think: I think my **paperwork** gets automated, but the trust will want an extra lesson in return.
The bigger worry is Priya, because **contract checking** is exactly what AI takes first.
do: Do the trust's **AI training** properly this time and get good at the tools.
Push the union for a rule that **saved time** stays with teachers.
Pause the **deposit** and keep four months as an emergency fund.
feel: **Fairly good** about his own job, with a **knot** in his stomach about Priya's.

fieldNote: The household risk sits with his **girlfriend's job**, not his own classroom.

steps.text: Complete the trust's AI training and use the marking tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what governments exist for: you don't let the market tear up schools and law firms in two years and shrug. I'd be calling for a pause and for wages to be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Priya loses her job first, probably in 2028, and I'm not far behind. A machine that can explain chemistry better than me, mark it, and track every kid's progress is most of what I'm paid for. The practicals keep me going a while, but a trust looking at costs might just make them videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away we'd stop saving for a flat and cut back to essentials, because a deposit means nothing if neither of us has a job. I'd get active in the union for real, not just paying dues. I'd use the AI tools every day to understand what they can do, because I'd rather know my enemy. And we'd shelve talk of getting married next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, like getting results day wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job has a lot of hands-on lab work. Does the three-year gap before robots matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a few years of lab supervision maybe. Someone has to stop a fourteen-year-old pouring acid in the sink, but that's a lab technician's job, at lower pay. And I'd be competing with every chemistry teacher in the country for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya the night you both realise this is happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a team and we'll work it out, and I'd mean it, but I'd also be lying awake. Then I'd say let's not book the wedding venue yet.

say: I'd say governments must **step in** and not let the market tear up schools in two years.
I'd call for a **pause** and for wages to be protected.
think: I think Priya **loses her job** first, around 2028, and I'm not far behind.
Practicals keep me going a while, but they may become **videos** or technician work.
do: Stop **saving for a flat** and cut spending to essentials.
Become **active in the union**, not just pay dues.
Shelve **wedding plans** for next year until we know where we stand.
feel: **Properly scared**, like getting results day badly wrong.
S2.quote: Someone has to stop a fourteen-year-old pouring acid in the sink, but that's a lab technician's job, at lower pay.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot gap** as a slide into lower-paid lab supervision, not a safe harbour.
Expects **both incomes** to go within a few years, which drives the alarm.
Uses AI daily here in order to **understand the threat**, a striking shift.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Join the union branch committee and attend every meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to plan this properly, and that means teachers and lawyers at the table, not just tech firms. I'd sign whatever petition was going round for a transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means I've got a few good years and then a real wobble at thirty-two. Priya has maybe three before her kind of work starts going. It's not the cliff edge, but it's a slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the AI tools over the next year, and maybe take on the trust's lead role for using them in science. I'd rather be the person who runs the system than the person replaced by it. We'd keep saving, aiming for six months, and Priya would start a part-time course in something less exposed, maybe employment law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, what's different about what you'd do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newer teachers who haven't got a shortage subject. History, English, maybe. And the teaching assistants, especially the older ones. They'd be the first to go if the budget gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether to start a family. I'm not sure I'd want to with a slope like that ahead. We'd likely wait until 2031 and see.

say: I'd say there's time to plan if **teachers and lawyers** are at the table, not just tech firms.
I'd sign any petition for a **transition fund** for affected workers.
think: I think I have a few **good years**, then a real wobble around thirty-two.
Priya has perhaps **three years** before her kind of legal work starts going.

Build savings to **six months** of bills.
Support Priya starting a part-time course in **employment law**.
feel: **Worried**, but in a way he can work with.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person who runs the system than the person replaced by it.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **positioning plan**: become the trust's AI lead.
He worries for **non-shortage teachers** and teaching assistants more than himself.

steps.text: Apply for the trust's science AI lead role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right if politicians actually try. Schools could keep teachers and use the machines for the drudge work, which is what everyone wanted in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think with a decade, the public will want humans in schools and it'll be protected, like nurses. I'd rather be a teacher than a solicitor in a world with ten years of warning. It's more Priya's career I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and slowly get better with AI, the way I did with the worksheets. I'd up my pension contributions a bit, since the trust matches it. And I'd vote for whoever promises a human teacher in every room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but not the knot I had with the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out, you'd be thirty-seven. How do you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of science somewhere, managing the AI and the practicals, hopefully with a kid of my own by then. Maybe living somewhere cheaper, out of town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm and alarmed in different pictures. Where does this one sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the middle. My job looks safe-ish, with plenty to think about. It's the not knowing what Priya will do that sits with me.

think: I think the public will want **humans in schools**, protected like nurses.
I'm more worried about **Priya's career** than my own.

Raise **pension contributions** while the trust matches them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us go at once. What would help is a proper income guarantee for a year or two while people retrain, and the government saying clearly that schools keep teachers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the practicals. Everyone thinks teaching is talking, but half of chemistry is making sure nobody loses an eyebrow. That's the bit I'd fight hardest to keep.

headlineQuote: Half of chemistry is making sure nobody loses an eyebrow.
portrait: Emeka is a **chemistry teacher** at a large academy who loves practicals and hates data drops.
He lives with his **girlfriend Priya**, a junior solicitor whose research work is highly exposed.
As a **steady adopter**, he uses AI for worksheets and would deepen that once it's proven.
He moves from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, when both incomes could go.
With more warning he aims to become the trust's **AI lead** in science.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his and Priya's incomes could go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee** for a year or two while people retrain.
A clear government promise that **schools keep teachers**.
